evidence.paraphrase: The narrator observes Sitka Charley's intense contemplation and is curious about it.
evidence.quote:
Something was going on in that
mind of his, and, whatever it was, I knew it was well worth
knowing.

evidence.paraphrase: Sitka Charley contrasts static pictures with life, saying pictures lack beginning and end.
evidence.quote:
That picture is all end,
" he said.
"It has no beginning.

evidence.paraphrase: Sitka Charley draws a distinction between life, where events resolve, and pictures, where nothing happens.
evidence.quote:
It is not life," he delivered himself
dogmatically.
"In life little girl die or get
well.

Something happen in life.

In picture nothing
happen.

evidence.paraphrase: Sitka Charley reasons from observed physical evidence to conclude the woman is crying rather than asleep.
evidence.quote:
Perhaps she is asleep," he repeated.

He
studied it closely.

"No, she is not asleep.

The
shoulders show that she is not asleep.

I have seen the
shoulders of a woman who cried.

evidence.paraphrase: Sitka Charley deduces details of the depicted card game from visible clues in the painting.
evidence.quote:
There are no chips on the table," Sitka Charley
explained.

"The men are playing with markers.
That means the roof is the limit.

evidence.paraphrase: The impending freeze-up of the waterways threatens to strand travelers and force a long overland journey.
evidence.quote:
Maybe one
day, maybe three days, maybe six days, any day maybe freeze-up
come, then no more water, all ice, everybody walk, Dawson six
hundred miles, long time walk.

evidence.paraphrase: Sitka Charley explains the physiological danger of breathing extreme cold air, causing lung damage and later illness.
evidence.quote:
Better that we
don	travel to-day," I say, "else will the
frost be unwarmed in the breathing and bite all the edges of our
lungs.

After that we will have bad cough, and maybe next
spring will come pneumonia.

evidence.paraphrase: Sitka Charley describes a moment of insight during hardship that changed his view of money and life.
evidence.quote:
And after that
never again do I care for money.

For that day a large
wisdom came to me.

There was a great light, and I saw
clear, and I knew that it was not for money that a man must live,
but for a happiness that no man can give, or buy, or sell

evidence.paraphrase: The travelers find McKeon dead in his snow-buried cabin, removing their expected food source.
evidence.quote:
I go
inside.

McKeon is dead.

Maybe two or three weeks he
is dead.

A sickness had come upon him so that he could not
leave the cabin.

The wind and the snow had covered the
cabin.

He had eaten his grub and died.
